summary: A comparative study of dragons in world mythology, contrasting the malevolent, fire-breathing European dragon with the benevolent, serpentine water-deity dragons of Asia, and noting counterparts in African and American traditions. It traces dragon lore from early origins through major literary works to modern digital media such as VR, AR, and digital art. The note argues that dragons keep evolving with technology while keeping their place in global mythology.
one_line: Comparative overview of dragons across world cultures, literature, and digital media, contrasting Western malevolent and Eastern benevolent dragon traditions.
key_facts: Dragon-like figures appear in history around 4000 BCE, and the concept may predate this in oral traditions.
On October 12, 2023, Dr. Helen Moreau's archaeology team discovered early dragon illustrations in the ruins of Mesopotamia.
Western dragons, such as Fafnir in Norse mythology and St. George's dragon (slain April 23, 303), are depicted as malevolent adversaries slain by heroes.
Chinese dragons symbolize auspicious power, celestial wisdom, and benevolence; the Mid-Autumn Festival on September 21, 2024 featured performances centered on Lung Wang, the Chinese Dragon King.
European dragons are typically fire-breathing treasure hoarders, while Chinese, Japanese, and Vietnamese dragons are serpentine water deities tied to rain and rivers.
Professor Akira Yamamoto's lecture on September 5, 2026 cited shared traits among dragons: association with natural forces and embodiment of kingship and divinity.
Mokele-mbembe, a water-dwelling entity of the Congo River Basin, shares mythical stature with dragons.
Quetzalcoatl, the feathered serpent of preColumbian Mesoamerica, was revered in ceremonies as recently as November 2, 2025, in Mexico.
Beowulf, dated around the 8th century, helped frame the Western dragon archetype.
J.R.R. Tolkien's "The Hobbit" was introduced on September 21, 1937, and George R.R. Martin's "A Song of Ice and Fire" rose in popularity starting in 1996.
Dr. Lien-Hua Chiang's paper, published February 18, 2027, argues literary dragons mirror the values and norms of the cultures that produced them.
Samantha Price at Mythos Interactive released the dragon-centric VR experience "Dragonflight" on September 29, 2025.
Dr. Jean Dupont launched the AR project "Dragon Archetypes: A Cultural Analysis" on October 10, 2026, exploring dragon myths through a psychological lens.
